title: Hand the terminal's chip data and PIN block to the host intact

blocks.text: The fuel stations' new pay-at-pump terminals talk to `TerminalBridge`, in `src/main/java/com/example/practice/TerminalBridge.java`. Their software sends everything as hex text, and the PIN pad driver hands over each PIN block in a buffer that it fills again for the next customer. The client sends to two hosts: the course's ASCII link and a second link whose packager treats field 55 as binary.
`purchase` already builds the request. Finish the three methods marked `TODO`:

items: `putChipData`: the chip's data into the request;
`putPinBlock`: the PIN block into the request;
`chipDataForTerminal`: the host's chip data, from field 55 of a response, back to the terminal.

blocks.text: When you're done, both hosts receive exactly the bytes the chip produced and the PIN block each customer typed, even when a request is packed after the next customer has used the PIN pad. The terminal gets the host's chip data as hex from either link, and `null` when the host sent none. About five lines in total.
The tests pack each message with the link's packager and unpack it again, as the other end does.

cases.says: a purchase reaches the host with the PIN block the cardholder typed
chip data in the host's response reaches the terminal as hex text
the host receives the chip's bytes, not the hex text the terminal handed over, on an ASCII link and on a binary one
a request keeps its own PIN block after the PIN pad reuses its buffer for the next cardholder
chip data unpacked as text by an ASCII packager still reaches the terminal as the hex of its bytes
a response without field 55 gives the terminal null rather than an exception

origin.section: 6.2 Binary Data Goes In as Bytes

concepts: An absent field reads as null from every getter but getMTI, so optional fields are read with a null check.
Binary data is set as bytes; a hex string becomes bytes only if a packager is attached when it is set, so in a client it goes out as text or fails to pack.
set(n, byte[]) keeps the caller's array, so a reused buffer changes a request that has not been packed yet.
